records.name: Nebraska
records.summary:
A gubernatorial executive order (August 30, 2023) narrows the legal definitions of 'male' and 'female', declares a person's biological sex fixed at birth, ends state recognition of transgender people, and backs single-sex spaces for bathrooms and changing rooms - mostly resident-facing, but it signals an administration willing to use state machinery against gender identity.

Below the national score 0.36.

sources.summary: NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (publisher returns 403 to automated fetches); the underlying Hill report covers the governor signing an executive order narrowing the legal definitions of 'male' and 'female' and ending state recognition of transgender people.

Governor's office announcement: on Aug. 30, 2023 Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen signed an executive order establishing the Women's Bill of Rights, making him the second U.S. governor to sign such an order 'declaring the biological definition of male and female.' The order backs single-sex spaces for women's sports, bathrooms and changing rooms and states that a person's biological sex is defined at birth. Primary state-government source for Nebraska's sex-definition policy.

Legal-news report: Nebraska Executive Order No. 23-16 signed Aug. 30, 2023 defines the terms sex, female, male, woman, girl, man, boy, mother and father for use by state agencies, stating there are biological differences between males and females in athletic abilities and safety that warrant sex-based segregation for some athletic, social and educational spaces. Reports that opponents questioned the order's scope and legality, and links the order text itself.

Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen signed an executive order on Aug. 30, 2023 establishing a Women's Bill of Rights, declaring a 'biological definition of male and female' and detailing the distinctions state agencies must apply. Local Nebraska news confirmation of the signing date and content of the executive order this record is about.

records.name: Montana
records.summary:
Montana has passed laws that would grade among the country's worst — including a facility-use ban and a public-buildings bathroom ban — but state courts have repeatedly blocked or enjoined them under the state constitution, leaving little of the anti-trans statutory book in force.

That makes Montana the anomaly of the 2026 legal-risk assessments: the only state whose risk grade was lowered — from 'worst laws' to 'high risk' — by cumulative court rulings and injunctions, in the February 2026 cycle. Statutory risk is high; enforcement risk is genuinely mixed.

sources.summary: July 2026 anti-trans national risk assessment: Montana is flagged as a special case — it has passed laws that would normally place it among the worst states, but those laws have been repeatedly blocked or enjoined under the state constitution, improving its standing on the assessment's rubric (which ranks states by expert reading of bills on adult and youth restrictions).

National risk assessment update: Montana is the single state that improves in the 2026 rankings, because the state court system has repeatedly blocked or enjoined anti-trans laws under the state constitution; adult restrictions that were passed have not taken full effect. Youth-side picture remains unstable nationally (federal policy shifts and litigation).

records.name: New Hampshire
records.summary: Highest per-capita incident load in the country: 72 recorded anti-LGBTQ incidents in 2025 in a state of ~1.4m. Counterweight: in July 2026 a county court found an attacker violated the NH Civil Rights Act after striking a trans gas-station employee, using his pronoun refusal as bias evidence, with bodycam showing officers correcting his pronoun use — institutions working. Slightly below the national score 0.36.

sources.summary: GLAAD 2025 national incident census: New Hampshire recorded 72 anti-LGBTQ incidents in 2025 — second-highest of any state after California (198), ahead of Texas (66), Ohio (50) and Washington (50).

Concord Monitor/NHPR (17 Jul 2026): Merrimack County Superior Court found a Concord man violated the New Hampshire Civil Rights Act by striking a transgender woman; republished by NHPR with the Granite State News Collaborative.

records.name: Arizona
records.summary:
A July 2026 national legal-risk assessment places Arizona among its 'low-risk states' group: it has largely refrained from targeting transgender adults, and although it has enacted policies affecting trans youth, the map's author considers them unlikely to be extended to adults. That is the assessment's praise of restraint, not of protection — no extraordinary protective measures are recorded for Arizona.

The local scene has tracked the national chill: Tucson cancelled its historic 2026 Pride celebration, citing a political and financial environment that made hosting nearly impossible and attending potentially unsafe.

sources.summary: July 2026 assessment: Arizona in its Low-Risk States group (AZ, DE, ME, MI, NV, PA, VA, WI, DC) — states that 'largely refrained from targeting transgender adults'; Arizona named alongside Virginia as having enacted youth-targeting anti-trans policies judged unlikely to be extended to adults.

Prism (3 Jun 2026): Tucson Pride cancelled all 2026 events in January and effectively dissolved, citing a political and financial environment that made supporting queer events nearly impossible; Tucson grouped with Tampa FL and Arlington TX as affected cities.

records.name: District of Columbia
records.summary: Downgraded from “most protective”: as a national district, the national legislature and the national executive reach it directly — the national legislature attached a bathroom ban for DC, and activists protesting it at the Capitol were arrested (December 2024). Its protective local-law layer persists but is overridable, and as of the September 2026 freshness confirmation DC itself has no facility ban and its protective code is unchanged; direction: mixed, downgraded from its former most-protective placement.

sources.summary: NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (Axios returned 403 to automated fetch); the underlying Axios report (5 Dec 2024) covers transgender-rights activists arrested while protesting at the Capitol against the bathroom ban Congress attached to the District of Columbia.

July 2026 assessment: DC may no longer be considered 'most protective' because it can fall under attack from Congress and executive actions; DC appears in the assessment's Low-Risk States list (AZ, DE, ME, MI, NV, PA, VA, WI, DC).

records.name: Maine
records.summary: Assessed comparatively protected (low-risk tier, July 2026) — but the state rose in risk after the University of Maine system capitulated to national pressure on trans sports participation rather than defending its trans students and athletes: the system affirmed compliance with the new national rules once the national agriculture department suspended its funding (March 2025). Direction: better than the country overall, with an upward risk signal.

sources.summary: July 2026 assessment: Maine in its Low-Risk States group, with the assessment separately flagging that Maine has increased in risk due to capitulation over sports bans in the University of Maine system.

NBC News (21 Mar 2025, upd. 24 Mar): University of Maine System announced compliance with federal restrictions on trans sports participation after the US Department of Agriculture suspended federal funding for research and programs while investigating possible sex-based discrimination in federally funded education programmes.
